Statement showing Economic Profile of the State in brief

As the Economic Survey brings out, the estimated percentage contribution of Agriculture &
allied, Industry and Service sectors are likely to be 19.36 per cent, 26.41 per cent, and 54.23
percent respectively in 2011-12 Advance estimates of GSDP at 2004-05 prices. In 2004-05, the
corresponding shares were 28.06 per cent, 28.22 per cent and 43.72 per cent, respectively.
Looking at the growth in different sectors of the State economy it is seen that real growth in
Agriculture and allied activities is estimated to be 2.28% over 2.00% in 2010-11, in Industry
4.65% (over 4.46% in 2010-11) and in Services 9.60% (over 9.70% in 2010-11). While the all-
round growth is a welcome sign, the Agriculture & Manufacturing sectors need greater impetus
for inclusive and sustainable growth. The State’s estimated GSDP for 2011-12 is about 0.70 per
cent of the country’s estimated Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for the year (@89,12,179 crore).
At current prices, Per Capita Income ( Per Capita Net State Domestic Product) was 30,212,
233,665, %37,496 and %41,833 for the years 2008-09, 2009-10, 2010-11 and 2011-12,
respectively, showing a steady increase, though still far short of the national average. In 2010-11,
the GSDP was assessed to be 47,709 crore as per Revised Estimates 2010-11 but in the final
reckoning the GSDP turned out to be significantly higher at 54,731 crore. In 2009-10 too, a
similar trend was noticed when the GSDP turned out to be %43,236 crore against projection of
%38,298 crore in the Revised Estimated 2009-10.As estimated by the Planning Commission of
India based on Consumer Expenditure Surveys, the Ratio of people Below Poverty Line (BPL)
to population in Jammu & Kashmir in 2004-05 was 5.4 per cent for total population (: 4.6 per
cent of Rural Population and 7.9 per cent of Urban population), the LOWEST poverty ratio
amongst all States. The absolute number of people Below Poverty was 5.9 lakh (€3.7 lakh Rural
and %2.2 lakh Urban). However, these estimates of the Planning Commission have not been
accepted by the State government. According to a BPL head count survey carried out by the
State government’s Directorate of Economics and Statistics in 2007-08, the total BPL Estimated
Population (Absolute Poverty) of J&K State was estimated to be 24.21 lakh persons (21.63 per
cent of total population) with a dispersion of 26.14 per cent (22.00 lakh persons) from Rural
areas and 7.96 per cent (2.21 lakh persons) living in Urban areas.The number of unemployed
registered with Employment Exchanges has increased/decreased from 1.09 lakh in 2006 to 5.97
lakh in 2010.The Statutory Minimum Wages effective from October 1, 2009 range from हैं 110
per day for unskilled labour to 7150 for semi-skilled and $200 per day for skilled labour.

1.5 Organisational structure of the office of the PAG (Audit), Jammu & Kashmir

Under the directions of the CAG, the Principal Accountant General (Audit), Jammu and.
Kashmir conducts audit of the State Government departments, Autonomous Bodies and
Government Companies. The Principal Accountant General (Audit) is assisted by three
Deputy Accountants General, Audit Officers, Assistant Audit Officers and supporting
staff in the discharge of his official duties.

During the year 2011-12, 42 audit parties comprising of 101 audit personnel and
supervised by Deputy Accountants General conducted audit of the selected units from
various departments of the State Government, autonomous bodies and externally aided
projects, etc.

1.6 Planning and conduct of audit

Audit process commences with the assessment of risk of various Government
departments/organizations/autonomous bodies and schemes/projects, etc., based on
expenditure, criticality/ complexity of activities, level of delegated financial powers,
assessment of internal controls and the concerns of stakeholders. The previous audit
findings are also considered as an input to this exercise.

After completion of audit of each unit, Audit Inspection Reports containing audit findings
are issued to the Head of the unit/ Department. The units are requested to furnish replies
to the audit findings within one month of receipt of the Audit Inspection Report.
Whenever replies are received, audit findings are either settled or further action for
compliance is advised. The important audit observations arising out of these Audit
Inspection Reports are processed for inclusion in the CAG’s Audit Report.

During 2011-12, 5525 party-days were utilised to carry out compliance audit of 825 units
out of 5905 units of various departments/organisations. The Audit Plan covered those
units/ entities which were vulnerable to significant risk, as per the assessment.

A. PERFORMANCE AUDIT

Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences

Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Medical Science (SKIMS) Srinagar was established in
December 1982 to provide specialized medical care, need based education in medical and
health services and clinical research and to develop referral linkage between primary,
secondary and tertiary health care in the State. The performance review revealed the
following financial and operational deficiencies:



Chapter-1-Intraduction

Financial deficiencies: The financial management was deficient as cases of under-
utilisation of funds, irregular withdrawals for crediting of funds to the Civil Deposit
heads and unauthorised retention and utilisation of hospital receipts were noticed in audit.
Operational deficiencies: The delivery of patient care services was affected by longer
waiting periods for diagnostic tests/ investigations and surgeries besides
mis-utilisation of ambulances meant for patients. The medical research activities had not
been attended to and the capacity of medical courses was not fully utilised. Audit also
noticed that the procurement system for purchase of drugs and equipment was deficient.
The quality and efficacy of drugs is sought to be ensured through higher priced
procurements and the funds released for setting up an Advanced Quality Assurance
Laboratory were lying unspent in a Civil Deposit. The hospital administration reported
that there were shortages of medical, paramedical and nursing staff and faculty though
the manpower requirements were not properly assessed/ benchmarked.

RURAL DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT
Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme

National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA) was notified by the Government of
India (GOD in September 2005 with the objective of enhancing livelihood security in
rural areas by providing at least 100 days of guaranteed wage employment in a financial
year to every household whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual labour.
The Act was extended to the State of Jammu and Kashmir with effect from May 2007.
The scheme was launched in the State in phases and gradually extended to all districts of
the State from April 2008. Out of the total number of 27.69 lakh Households in the State,
number of Households provided employment ranged between 1.44 lakh (five per cent)
and 5.67 lakh (20 per cent) during 2007-12. A performance review of the scheme by
Audit brought to fore several areas of concern such as non-observance of programme
guidelines in terms of nature of works to be taken up, unauthorized retention of funds,
delayed release and diversion of funds, execution of unapproved works, abandonment of
works, preparation of faulty estimates, delays in payment of wages to the workers,
shortfall in engagement of staff and their inadequate training, inadequate inspection of
works and social audit for proper monitoring of scope, extent and quality of works
executed and retention of undisbursed balances in the State Employment Guarantee Fund.

POWER DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT
Power Transmission Utilities

The National Electricity Policy recognized the need for continued development of
National Grid for providing adequate infrastructure for inter-state transmission of power.
Both the Central Transmission Utility (CTU) and the State Transmission Utility (STU)
have the key responsibility of network planning and development based on the National
Electricity Plan in coordination with all the concerned agencies. The transmission of
electricity and Grid operations in the State are managed and controlled by the Power



Audit Report on Social, General, Revenue and Economic Sectors (Non-PSUs) for the year ended 31 March 2012

Development Department. The Performance Audit of Transmission utilities in the State
revealed under-utilisation of plan funds and non-achievement of targets in capacity
additions in respect of grid sub-stations and transmission lines. Almost all the Grid sub-
stations and Transmission Line projects witnessed a time over-run due to inadequate
planning, faulty designs etc. Some of the completed projects could not be operationalised
due to incompletion of related works, with the result that the infrastructure created was
lying idle. The transmission losses in the State exceeded the Central Electricity Authority
(CEA) norm of four per cent during the period 2008-12. Due to in-efficient Grid
management, the State Government had to pay the unscheduled Interchange charges. The
disaster management setup did not exist in the Department for immediate restoration of
transmission system in the event of major failures.

B. THEMATIC AUDIT
LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT DEPARTMENT

Functioning of J&K Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board

Government of India (GOT) enacted (August 1996)> the Building and Other Construction
Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1996 (BOCW Act)
for constitution of a Welfare Board in each State to undertake social security schemes’.
The GOI also enacted (August 1996)’ the Building and Other Construction Workers
Welfare Cess Act, 1996 (Cess Act). Section 14 of the Cess Act stipulates that rule
making power under the Act vests only with the GOI. The GOI framed (March 1998) the
Building and other Construction Workers’ Welfare Cess Rules, 1998 (Cess Rules). To
augment the resources of the Board, Section 3 of the Cess Act as amended in
September 1996 provided for levy and collection of labour welfare cess at a uniform rate
of one per cent of the cost of construction incurred by the employer. For the safety,
health and welfare of the workers, the State Government in pursuance of sections 40 and
62 of the BOCW Act also framed (July 2006) the Jammu and Kashmir Building and
Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service)
Rules, 2006 (J&KBOCW Rules) as amended in November 2012. The State Government
constituted (July 2007) the Jammu and Kashmir Building and Other Construction
Workers Welfare Board (Board) to carry out welfare schemes for construction workers.
Audit scrutiny revealed delay in constitution of Board resulting in non-enforcement of the
pro’ ms of the Act for the social security and other welfare measures of workers
besides loss of cess to the Board. Against the available funds of हैं 104.52 crore, the Board
utilized हैं 3.90 crore (four per cent) during 2010-12, leaving an unspent balance of
& 100.62 crore as at the end of 31 March 2012. Besides, cases of delay in submission of
cheques valuing of ~ 95.60 lakh on account of cess money, expenditure on administrative
expenses in violation of the provisions of the Act and non preparation of annual reports
for the financial years 2010-11 and 2011-12 were also noticed in audit.

2.1.3 Governing structure of the Institute

The functioning of the Institute is overseen by a high level Governing Body (GB)
ired by the Hon’ble Chief Minister of the State. The GB has some Cabinet
members, with the Director of the Institute as Member Secretary. The
Chief Secretary and other Administrative Secretaries act as advisors. The GB is
assisted by Apical Selection Committee (ASC) chaired by the Chief Secretary to
handle appointment/ promotion of faculty and Standing Finance Committee (SFC)
chaired by the Financial Commissioner to look after financial matters. Besides, there
are Senior Selection Committee (SSC) and Junior Selection Committee (JSC) chaired
by the Director of the Institute to look after appointment/ promotion of Gazetted and
Non-Gazetted staff, respectively. Other committees include Standing Academic
Committee, Purchase Committee, Works Contract Committee, Technical Committee
for purchase of drugs, etc. The Director is designated as ex-officio Secretary to
Government of the State for matters related to the Institute. The decisions taken by the
Governing Body are deemed to have approval of the Cabinet, conveyed by issuing
Government orders by the Director in his capacity of ex-officio Secretary to the
Government. The Institute was granted statutory status to function as a deemed
university to award degrees in medical and allied specialties from August 1983 under
the provisions of the Sher-i-Kashmir Institute of Medical Sciences (Grant of Degrees)

Act, 1983. The Institute’s medical education/ research activities are also covered by
the regulatory mechanism of the Indian Council of Medical Research. Thus, the
Institute has attributes of an autonomous statutory body, a deemed university and an
entity having the powers of a Government Department without the usual system of
checks and balances applicable to a Government Department. The unique governing
structure, while designed to facilitate its functioning, casts special responsibilities on
the administration of the Institute.

2.1.8 Planning

Strategic planning is necessary for attaining the long term goals of an entity in a time-
bound frame work. It forms the core of an implementation process. A properly
planned approach for infrastructure development and purchase of medical equipment
taking into account the needs and preferences of professionals and end users for
retaining consistency and control is needed for ensuring value for money. This may be
achieved by preparing a long term perspective plan for implementation in a phased
manner.

Audit noticed that the Institute did not have any approved long term master/
perspective Plan for phased and planned infrastructure development and purchase of
medical equipment or civil infrastructure. Thus, build-up of infrastructure (Civil
Works and Equipment) and matching manpower profile was based on requirements
projected from time to time. Even the draft Annual Plans prepared by the Institute
were not adhered to and % 24.09 crore was incurred on unplanned works during
2007-12 as brought out in Paragraph 2.1.9 below.

The Institute had prepared 11th Five Year Plan period (2007-12) proposals amounting
to = 214.05 crore which was subsequently reduced to हैं 146.14 crore on the basis of
fresh ceiling conveyed by the Planning & Development Department, Government of
Jammu and Kashmir. The supporting statements in respect of plan proposals under
infrastructure development and equipment were not available with the Planning Wing
of the Institute. The annual plans prepared could not thus be correlated with the 11th
Five Year Plan projections.

2.1.12.2 Purchase of drugs

The requirement of drugs are assessed annually on the basis of the requisitions of
various medical departments. The quantities of different kinds of medicines to be
procured are determined after taking into account the available balance of
unconsumed drugs in central stores of the Institute. A health care system can ill-afford
to purchase drugs mentioned under different proprietary brands at widely varying
prices. A limited list of essential drugs also referred to as drug formulary defines
which drugs will be regularly purchased. At the core of the concept is the objective
that procurement should be limited to drugs that are economically priced but safe and
effective.

It was noted that a formal system of pre and post-qualification of prospective
suppliers to ensure procurement from suppliers of quality products was not in place.

The SKIMS Purchase Committee in its meeting held on 16% July 2007 had desired
that instead of open tender system for drugs, the Institute should come up with a
proposal for purchase on the pattern of ATIMS, Delhi. The Finance Department
conveyed (February 2008) approval of the Chairman Governing Body to the proposal.
There was delay in implementing the new purchase policy and the earlier contract was
extended upto December 2008. Under the new system, the manufacturing companies
were to be short listed in consultation with Heads of Departments and rates invited
from them for a two year rate contract effective from February 2009, later extended
upto March 2012. The rates achieved under the new purchase policy were generally
lower both in respect of Sale Counter Drugs and Hospital drugs. However, the
purchase of 29 drugs for Sale Counter Drugs from April 2008 to December 2008 on
old rate contract resulted in excess expenditure of = 10.91 lakh.

The pharmaceutical procurement procedure should normally include, wherever
practicable, identification of generic over proprietary drugs. The Government of India
in association with the Central Pharma Public Sector Undertakings has launched a
campaign for opening Jan Aushadhi stores where unbranded quality generic
medicines would be sold at lower prices, though equivalent in potency to branded
expensive drugs. Thus, with the same cost, ten times more persons could be treated
with same efficacy and cure. No effort was, however, made to open Jan Aushadhi sale
outlet in the Institute or procure generic medicines under the programme. The
Director of the Institute stated (December 2012) that the Institute has its own Drug
Sales Counter which sells medicines at cheaper and economical rates and that the
opening of Jan Aushadhi outlet in SKIMS was subject to authorization of the
Governing Body

The system of drawing of samples of drugs for testing to ensure procurement of
quality medicines and drugs is not in vogue in the Institute. For exercising quality
control, both the options of having an in-house quality control set up and buying from

2.2.1 Introduction

The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA) was notified by the
Government of India (GOI) in September 2005 with the objective of enhancing
livelihood security in rural areas by providing at least 100 days of guaranteed wage
employment in a financial year to every household whose adult members volunteer to
do unskilled manual work. The Act is a right based framework for adult members of a
tural household willing to do unskilled manual work. It prescribes time bound
guarantee wherein if employment is not provided within 15 days from the date of
application for work, the State Government has to give unemployment allowance. The
Act was extended to the State of Jammu and Kashmir with effect from May 2007. The
programme which became effective from February 2006 was initially launched in
three’ districts of the State in the first phase and extended to two” more districts in
the year 2007-08 and to all the districts of the State from April 2008. The programme
was rechristened as Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme

e Enhancing the livelihood security of people in rural areas by guarantecing

© Creation of a strong social safety net for vulnerable groups by providing a fall-

e Strengthening of the natural resource base of rural livelihood and create durable
assets in rural areas through the process of providing employment on works that

e Exercising transparency and grass-root democracy in governance.

2.2.6 Structural mechanisms

For implementation of the programme in accordance with provisions of the Act,
structural mechanism had to be put in place and adequate capacity building
measures to be taken both by the GOI and the State Government. The State
Government had to formulate rules and the Gram Panchayats at the Village level had
to be made pivotal bodies for implementation of the programme from planning to
execution and monitoring level. The responsibility of formulation of plans and
Labour Budget for monitoring and supervision of the programme at the District level
was to be entrusted to District Panchayats, to be formed at District level, with a view
to ensuring public participation in developmental works.

For implementation of the programme, the State Government notified the Jammu
and Kashmir Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme in March 2007. The Panchayats
in the State came into being with effect from June 2011 after the Panchayat elections
conducted during the period March-June 2011. Till then the role of the Panchayats
for identification of the works for execution in a village was taken over by the
Blocks through Village Level Workers (VLWs). No Intermediate Panchayats at
Block level and no District Panchayats at District level were in existence in the State
(March 2012). The Annual Action Plans (AAPs) formulated at the Panchayat/ Block

2.2.6.1 Constitution of State Employment Guarantee Council

For the purpose of regular monitoring and reviewing the implementation of the Act
at the State level, the State Government was required to constitute a Jammu and
Kashmir State Employment Guarantee Council which was to meet at least twice in a
year. The State Employment Guarantee Council (SEGC) was constituted by the
Government in March 2006 with Hon’ble Chief Minister of the State as Chairperson
of the Council. However, from September 2008 Minister-in-charge for Rural
Development was nominated as Chairperson ex-officio of SEGC. The SEGC held
only three meetings (March 2008, January 2010 and April 2011) during the period
2007-12 against the requirement of 10 meetings. It was observed that the decisions
taken by the SEGC in the meetings had been implemented partially. The decisions
regarding strengthening of State MGNREGS Cell, appointment of requisite staff
under the scheme and of consultants at the State/ District level for quality
monitoring, routing of funds through State Employment Guarantee Fund etc. had not
been implemented as of March 2012. Due to non-appointment of consultants at the
State level, the MGNREGs Cell which was to provide technical support in the key
areas like Information Education and Communication strategies, training needs,
planning, monitoring and evaluation, social audit and financial management under
the scheme could not look into these key areas. Further, the Annual Report on the
state of affairs of implementation of the programme in the State could not be
brought out and tabled in the State Legislature. The Member Secretary (SEGC)
stated (October 2012) that the Annual Reports for the period from 2007-08 to
2010-11 would be printed out in a consolidated form to be presented in the next
session of the Assembly.

2.2.6.2 Constitution of State Employment Guarantee Fund (SEGF)

For the purpose of implementation of the scheme, the State Government had to
establish a State Employment Guarantee Fund (SEGF). The State Government
accordingly established (October 2008) a separate Bank account for the scheme in
Jammu and Kashmir Bank Limited, Civil Secretariat but the SEGF had not been made
fully operational and the particulars of the fund were not communicated to the GOI.
As a result, the funds were released by the GOI directly to the districts for
implementation of the programme. This defeated the very purpose of establishment of
SEGF. An amount of हैं 17.20 lakh released by the GOI in June 2008 had been
deposited in the fund account. Further, = 15 crore released by the State Government
on account of difference in the wages of the beneficiaries due to enhancement in wage
rates retrospectively had been deposited in the fund account in July 2010. As the
wages had not been paid to the beneficiaries, the amount alongwith interest of = 15.81

during exit conference stated (November 2012) that proposal to convert undisbursed

2.2.7 Planning

Planning is the main tool for successful implementation of a programme. The
Programme guidelines provide for preparation of perspective plans (PP) by the
districts to facilitate advance planning and to provide a development perspective for
the district. A district perspective plan for five years would have the advantage of
facilitating the annual labour budgets as a framework of long term planning and
would enable the adoption of a project approach to works. The Annual Development
Plans (ADP) which would flow from the PPs would be working plans that contain
the nature, number and nomenclature of the developmental works to be executed in
a year. For this purpose, the involvement of the Gram Panchayats was to be made
mandatory for identification of works. Based on such identification, the ADPs had to
be drawn, which would be converted into Labour Budget (LB) in financial terms at
the Block, District and the State level for transmission to the GOI for release of
funds. Timely submission of LBs to the GOI was, as such, necessary for release of
funds in time. Following points were observed in audit.

2.2.7.1 Non-formulation of Perspective Plans

Audit observed that none of the test-checked districts had formulated PPs during the
period of review except for three districts (Udhampur, Rajouri and Leh) where the
PPs had been formulated belatedly from the year 2010-11. The MS (SEGC) stated
(November 2012) that PPs had been formulated by all the districts. The reply is quite
contrary to the factual position of formulation of PPs by the test-checked districts. In
the absence of PPs, the advance planning to provide developmental perspective for
the district could not be achieved.

2.2.7.2 Delayed/Non-submission of Labour Budget

As per the programme guidelines, the Gram Panchayats have to identify and
recommend the works in the Gram Sabha to be held on 2 October for execution in
the ensuing year and forward the development plan to the Programme Officer (PO)
by 15 October every year. The PO has to scrutinize, re-refer the plan to Gram
Panchayats, if necessary, and consolidate the plan and submit the same to
Intermediate Panchayat (at Block level) by 15 November which has to approve the
Block Plan within 15 days for submission to the District Programme Coordinator
(DPC) by 30 November. The DPC has to submit the Block-wise shelf of projects
and the Labour Budget (LB) thereon to the District Panchayat Officer (DPO) by 15
December. After getting it approved by the District Panchayat by 31 December, the
DPC has to forward the LB to the State Government, which will forward it
alongwith its recommendations to the GOI by 31 January.

Audit, however, observed that records regarding submission of the plans by the
Panchayats to the blocks were not available in any of the test-checked Panchayats.
Test-checked blocks in two districts (Rajouri and Udhampur) had submitted the LBs
to the DPC after delays of two to three months. The details/records of submission of
LBs were not available in other blocks of four test-checked districts. Similarly no
records/details regarding submission of LBs during the period 2007-10 to the GOT
were available with the MS (SEGC). However, Audit noticed that submission of
LBs to the GOI by the State Government had been delayed by two months during
each year 2010-11 and 2011-12. The MS (SEGC) stated (October 2012) that the

Annual LB was submitted to the GOI on the basis of which, the State was able to
seek the Central assistance under the scheme.

2.2.7.3 Convergence of scheme funds

The programme guidelines provide for convergence of scheme funds with the funds
from other sources such as Finance Commission, Centrally Sponsored Schemes like
Swaranjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yogna (SGSY), Drought Prone Area Programme
(DPAP), Desert Development Programme (DDP), etc. for construction of durable
community assets/works permissible under the scheme. Special guidelines for this
purpose had to be issued by the State Government. Audit did not observe any action
having been taken at any level in this direction by the Department. It was, however,
seen that a Committee had been constituted (March 2012) at the State level to look
into this aspect. The Commissioner-Secretary stated (November 2012) that the
mechanism of convergence of various schemes was not followed by the Department.

2.2.9.10 Unrealistic estimation of works

The framing of estimates before execution of a work is an utter necessity as it gives
an insight into the technical parameters of the work besides the actual idea of the
quantum of funds required for the scheme. The estimates of each work are thus
required to be framed meticulously.

It was, however, seen that huge variations existed between the estimates of works
and the actual spending thereon. In nine” blocks of five’’ districts, 672 works
estimated to cost = 10.45 crore taken up for execution during the period 2007-12 had
been completed at a cost of हैं 3.52 crore which constituted 34 per cent of the
estimated cost. The variation between the estimates and the actual expenditure in
case of individual works ranged between 20 and 73 per cent. This is indicative of the
casual approach of the technical staff of the department in framing of estimates
without verification of the site conditions leading to unrealistic estimation. The
BDOs Mendhar and Poonch attributed (June 2012) this to availability of
construction material near the sites of works executed and also due to some changes
in site conditions. The BDO Udhampur stated (April 2012) that the technical staff
would be asked to explain the position. The replies are not acceptable as framing of
unrealistic estimates lead to misrepresentation of facts in the AAPs with direct
bearing on funding.

2.2.9.11 Procurement of construction material

As per the GOI instructions (November 2010), the State Government had to frame a
procurement policy at the State level for procurement of key construction material
for the works. It was however seen that no uniform procurement policy was in place
in the State and procurement of construction material was being made from different
sources at District/ Block levels. The Director, RDD, Jammu had directed (October
2010) ACDs to procure material from Stores Procurement Department (SPD). The
non-uniformity in procurement of construction material was visible from the fact
that the executing agencies in Kashmir Division had procured material from JK
Cements Limited whereas in Jammu Division, the executing agencies had carried
out procurement from JAKFED and SICOP. The ACD, Poonch stated (June 2012)
that construction material is procured from SICOP/JAKFED which supplies it
within the shortest possible time as compared to the SPD which supplies the
material late. The BDOs, Rajouri and Chenani stated (April 2012) that the material
is procured from other sources when not available with SPD. The fact however
remains that no uniform policy had been framed to ensure procurement in a
transparent manner. The MS (SEGC) informed that the Directors at the divisional
level had been advised (April 2012) to formulate the procurement policy.

POWER DEVELOPMENT DEPARTME

2.3 Power Transmission Utilities
Executive Summary

The National Electricity Policy (NEP) recognized the need for continued
development of National Grid for providing adequate infrastructure for
inter-state transmission of power. Both the Central Transmission Utility
(CTU) and the State Transmission Utility (STU) have the key
responsibility of network planning and development based on the
National Electricity Plan (NEP) in coordination with all the concerned
agencies. The transmission of electricity and Grid operations in the State
are managed and controlled by the Power Development Department.
The Performance Audit of Transmission utilities in the State revealed
under-utilisation of plan funds and non-achievement of targets in
capacity additions in respect of Grid sub-stations and Transmission
lines. Almost all the Grid sub-stations and Transmission line projects
witnessed a time over-run due to inadequate planning, faulty designs etc.
Some of the completed projects could not be operationalised due to
incompletion of related works, with the result the infrastructure created
was lying idle. The transmission losses in the State exceeded the Central
Electricity Authority (CEA) norm of four per cent during the period
2008-12. Due to in-efficient Grid management the State Government had
to pay the Unscheduled Interchange (UI) charges. The disaster
management setup did not exist in the Department for immediate
restoration of transmission system in the event of major failures.

The Department transmitted 8,010 Million Units (MU) of energy during
2007-08 which increased by 29 per cent to 10,367 MU in 2011-12 while as
the transmission network installed capacity increased from 4,489 Mega
Volts Ampere (MVA) in 2007-08 to 7,273 MVA in 2011-12.

(Paragraph: 2.3.6)
The Department had not formulated the State Electricity Policy and
State Electricity Plan.

(Paragraph: 2.3.7)

2.3.1 Introduction

With a view to ensure availability of reliable and quality power to all by the
year 2012, the Government of India (GOI) notified the National Electricity
Policy (NEP) in February 2005 which inter-alia stated that the Trans1 ion
System required adequate and timely investment besides efficient and
coordinated action to develop a robust and integrated power system for the
country, The NEP also, recognized the need for continued development of
National Grid for providing adequate infrastructure for inter-state
transmission of power. Both the Central Transmission utility (CTU) and the
State Transmission utility (STU) have the key responsibility of network
planning and development based on the National Electricity Plan in
coordination with all the concerned agencies. In the State of Jammu and
Kashmir, transmission of electricity and Grid operations are managed and
controlled by Jammu and Kashmir Power Development Department (PDD)
which is also responsible for planning and development of the intra-state
transmission system.

62

2.3.2 Organizational Structure

The State Power Development Department is headed by the Principal
Secretary and the day to day activities of the Department are carried out by
the Development Commissioner, Power (DCP) who is assisted by two Chief
Engineers (CE), System & Operation (S&O) Wings one each for Jammu and
Kashmir besides, one CE, Planning and Design Wing and one CE,
Commercial and Survey Wing. The S&O Wing is responsible for execution
of various transmission projects and the Planning and Design Wing of the
Department studies and finalizes technical parameters of the projects for their
approval besides, planning of infrastructure and procurement of key material
required for the transmission projects. The Commercial and survey wing
deals with the purchase of power and manages operations of the State Load
Despatch Centres of the Department. The four CEs are assisted by seven
Superintending Engineers (SEs), who in tum are assisted by the 19 Executive
Engineers acting as divisional heads

2.3.3. Audit Objectives

The objectives of the performance audit were to assess whether:

e Perspective Plan was prepared in accordance with the guidelines of the
National Electricity Policy/Plan and State Electricity Regulatory
Commission (SERC);

e The transmission system was developed, commissioned and maintained
in an economical, efficient and effective manner;

e Disaster Management System was set up to safeguard its operations
against unforeseen disruptions;

e Effective failure analysis system was set up;
e Effective and efficient Financial Management system existed;

e Efficient and effective system of procurement of material and inventory
control mechanism existed; and

e <A monitoring system was in place to review functioning of the
transmission projects and to take corrective measures wherever

2.3.6 Power Transmission infrastructure

The transmission of electricity is defined as bulk transfer of power over long
distances at high voltages, generally at 132 Kilo Volts (KV) and above. The
electric power generated at relatively low voltages in power plants is stepped
up to high voltage power before it is transmitted to reduce the loss in
transmission and to increase efficiency in the Grid. Sub-stations (SSs) are
facilities within the high voltage electric system used for stepping-
up/stepping down voltages from one level to another, connecting electric
systems and switching equipment in and out of the system. The step up
transmission SSs at the generating stations use transformers to increase the
voltages for transmission over long distances. Transmission lines carry high
voltage electric power and the step down transmission SSs_ thereafter
decreases voltages to sub transmission voltage levels [66/33/11 Kilo Volts
Ampere (KVA)] for distribution to consumers. The distribution system
includes lines, poles, transformers and other equipment needed to deliver
electricity at specific voltages. Electrical energy cannot be stored; hence
generation of power must be matched to the requirement. Therefore, every
transmission system requires a sophisticated system of control called Grid
management to ensure balancing of power generation closely with demand.

2.3.9 Project management of transmission network

A transmission project involves various activities from concept to
commissioning stage through Project formulation, appraisal/approval phase
and Project execution phase. For reduction in project implementation period,
the Ministry of Power, Government of India (GOI) constituted (February
2005) a Task Force on transmission projects to suggest and recommend
measures to curtail delays in project implementation so that the projects are
completed on schedule and chances of time-over-run and cost-over-run are
eradicated. The Task Force recommended (August 2005) the following
remedial actions:

* to undertake various preparatory activities such as surveys, design &
testing, processing for forest & other statutory clearances, tendering
activities etc. in advance/parallel to project appraisal and approval phase
and go ahead with construction activities once transmission line project
sanction/approval is received;

e to break-down the transmission projects into clearly defined packages
such that the packages can be procured & implemented requiring least
coordination & interfacing and at same time it attracts competition
facilitating cost effective procurement; and

standardize designs prior to floating of tenders for tower fabrication so
that 6-12 months or more time can be saved in project execution.

Though the implementation of transmission projects upto the year 2003
continued mostly through State Plan, the power sector got boost with the
announcement of Prime Minister's Reconstruction Plan (PMRP) in
November 2004 for the State. Audit scrutiny of records (April 2012) of the
Chief Engineer, S&O Wing revealed that for development of transmission
infrastructure in the State a project estimated to cost of = 707 crore was
formulated (2003) by the State Government and sent to the Ministry of
Power, Government of India (501) for approval under 10" five year Plan
period (2002-07). The cost of the project involving 66 works which included
construction of 24 Grid sub-stations (GSS) laying of 37 Transmission lines
(TLs) and augmentation of the existing five sub-stations was revised to
= 1,006.46 crore in September 2004 after its scrutiny by Central Electricity
Authority (CEA). The project cost was further revised (2006) to हैं 1,351
crore due to substantial increase in cost of basic material viz. steel, cement
and transmission equipments. Further, 36 schemes/works of the project
(GSS: 17, TL: 19) were executed on turnkey basis through contractors and 30
schemes/works (GSS: seven, TL: 18, Augmentation works: five) were
executed departmentally.

Audit further observed that though the funds under the PMRP started flowing
in March 2005, the tendering activities in respect of turnkey projects were
commenced after a delay of two years and the letters of award for contracts
were issued from December 2007 onwards by the Department. The
consultancy for the project under PMRP was sought from CEA in January
2005 but the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the

2.3.11.3 Voltage management

According to Jammu and Kashmir Electricity Grid code, the utility is
required to maintain Grid voltage of 200-245 KV and 120-145 KV at bus
bars of the Grid sub-station ranging between 360 KV and 420 KV and 400
KV transmission lines between 220 KV and 132 KV transmission lines
respectively.

A test-check of records revealed that out of ten 220/132 KV Grid sub stations
in the State, the minimum bus voltage recorded at Gladni Grid sub-station
was 175 KV below the minimum required voltage limit of 200 KV.
Similarly, 28 Grid sub-stations out of 44 Grid sub-stations (132/33 KV), had
the minimum bus voltage below the required minimum level which ranged
between 96 and 119. This indicated that the grid voltages had not been

2.3.11.4 Extra High Voltage Transmission Lines (EHT)

As per Manual of Transmission Planning Criteria (MTPC), permissible line
loading cannot normally be more than the Thermal Loading Limit (TLL).
These limits restrict sag and loss of tensile strength of the transmission lines
and limit the maximum power flow of the lines. As per MTPC, the TLL of
132 KV line with Aluminum Conductor Steel Reinforced (ACSR) Panther
210 sq.mm conductor should be 366 amperes (amps). A test-check of records
revealed that the thermal loading in respect of 84 outgoing feeders (33KV
voltage level) of 19 Grid sub-stations had exceeded the thermal loading limit
of 366 amps which ranged between 370 amps to 2,210 amps. The loading of
the lines beyond the prescribed limits resulted in voltage fluctuations, higher
transmission losses and frequent interruptions/breakdowns.

2.3.11.5 Bus Bar Protection Panel (BBPP)

Bus bar is used as an application for interconnection of the incoming and
outgoing transmission lines and transformers at an electrical Sub-station. The
Bus bar protection panel (BBPP) limits the impact of the bus bar faults on the
entire power net-work which prevents unnecessary tripping and selective to
trip only those breakers necessary to clear the bus bar fault. As per Grid
norms and Best Practices in Transmission system, BBPP is to be kept in
service for all 220/132 KV Sub-stations to maintain system stability during
Grid disturbances and to provide faster clearance of faults on 220/132 KV
bus bars.

Test-check of records revealed that out of ten 220/132 KV Sub-stations only
two Grid sub-stations at Budgam and Bishnah were provided with BBPP.
The position with regard to the protection given to 44 Sub-stations at voltage
level of 132/33 KV was more dismal because only two* Grid sub-stations

2.3.12 Maintenance of Transmission system

The regular and periodic maintenance of transmission system is of utmost
importance for its un-interrupted operation. The Report of the Committee for
updating the Best practices of Transmission in the country, apart from
scheduled patrolling of lines, has prescribed various techniques for
maintenance of lines which include hot line maintenance, washing, puncture
detection of insulators, besides preventive maintenance by using portable
carthling hot line tools, vibration measurement of the line, thermo-scanning
and pollution measurement of the equipment. The hot line technique
envisages attending to maintenance works like hot spots, tightening of nuts
and bolts, damages to the conductor, replacement of insulators etc. of lines
without switching off and includes thermo scanning of all the lines for
preventive maintenance.

Audit observed (April 2012) that no hot line maintenance and washing
practice was adopted by the Department in the State. Further during test-
check, it was observed that the yard equipment viz. Power current
transformers, switch gears, circuit breaches installed at three Grid sub-
stations (Janipur, Udhampur and Gladni) had outlived their lives as these
were installed 25-30 years back. No action had been taken to either replace

2.3.14 Grid management

Transmission and Grid management are essential functions for smooth
evacuation of power from generating stations to the Distribution
utilities/consumers. Grid management ensures moment-to-moment power
balance in the interconnected power system to take care of reliability,
security, economy and efficiency of the power system. Grid management in
the State is carried out in accordance with the standards/directions given in
the Grid Code issued by SERC. The State Load Despatch Centre (SLDC), a
constituent of Northern Regional Load Despatch Centre (RLDC), New Delhi,
ensures integrated operation of power system in the State. The SLDC,
Jammu i: sted by Sub Load Despatch Centre situated at Bemina, Srinagar
for data acquisition and transfer to SLDC and supervisory control of 132 KV
and 33 KV equipments. The SLDC levies and collect such fees and charges
from the generating companies and licensees engaged in intra-state
transmission of electricity as specified by the SERC.

2.3.14.1 Infrastructure for load monitoring

Remote Terminal Units (RTUs)/Sub-station Management Systems (SMSs)
are essential for monitoring the efficiency of the transmission system and the
power loads during emergency in load dispatch centers as per the Grid norms
for all SSs. Audit observed (June 2012) that only eleven® Sub-stations (20
per cent) out of 54 Sub-stations were provided with RTUs for recording real
time data for efficient Energy Management System.

2.3.14.2. Grid discipline by frequency management

As per Grid Code, the transmission utilities are required to maintain Grid
discipline for efficient functioning of the Grid. All the constituent members
of the Grid are expected to maintain a system frequency between 49 and 50.5
Hertz (Hz).

For maintenance of Grid discipline, the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (CERC) takes up suo-motu petition on over drawal of power
from the Grid at a lower frequency thus putting the Grid to the risk.
According to the CERC, regulation (December 2002) on availability based
tariff (ABT) the State overdrawing/under drawing power than their scheduled
quota have to pay revenue charges at rates depending upon frequency. The
Unscheduled Interchange (UI) charges are payable for deviations from the
schedule and are also subject to the grid conditions at that point of time. The
levying of UI charges is a commercial mechanism to maintain grid
discipline.

2.3.14.3 Non-installation of capacitors

The power load demand in the State is being met with the availability of
power from self generation share in central sector power projects and power
purchased from the Northern Grid. The State mostly depends upon the
drawal of power from Northern Grid and due to excessive drawal of reactive
power the system voltage is substantially low. Reactive power is a concept to
describe the background energy movement in an alternating current system
arising from production of electric and magnetic fields. These fields store
energy which changes through each AC cycle. Devices which store energy
by virtue of electric fields are said to generate reactive power such as, electric
motors, welding sets, etc. The dissipation of power due to such devices
reduces power factor (ratio of real power to apparent power) and has to be
made up by way of devices which store energy by virtue of magnetic field
and are said to absorb reactive power such as capacitors. Consumers with a
power factor below 96 per cent are assessed with reactive power measured in
Kilo Volt Ampere Reactive (KVAR) charge. In order to improve the power
factor and the system voltage profile and also to reduce the drawal of reactive
current from the Northern Grid, all State Electricity Boards were asked to
install shunt capacitors in their respective networks.

The State Government had entered into an agreement (January 1979) with
Punjab State Government for sharing power and irrigation water share of
Ranjit Sagar Dam (Thein dam) project on river Ravi. The said agreement was
signed by the then Chief Ministers of the two States. The Thein dam houses
four generating units of 150 MVA each and has a total generating capacity of
600 MVA. The agreement between the two States provided that the State
Government would get share of 20 per cent in the total power generated at
Thien dam by the Punjab Government at the cost of generation at bus bars
and that in case the State Government was unable to utilize the aforesaid
share of power within its territory or was desirous of selling the same, the
surplus power would be sold to Punjab Government at mutually agreed rate.

To evacuate share of power from Thein Dam hydro electric project, the
Department took up construction of 220 KV double circuit, Thein- Hiranagar
transmission line during the period 1992-95. The single circuit of the line
was completed in the year 2005 at a cost of € 20.45 crore. The balance work
for second circuit of the transmission line was got approved under PMRP at a
cost of € 5.71 crore in the year 2006 and the work of 40.35 kms out of 41.54
km of projected length was completed (March 2010) at a cost of € 5.28 crore.
The Punjab Government also agreed to connect this transmission line to
Shahpur Kandi switchyard subject to the condition that the State Government
would bear the cost (% 4.5 crore) of two number 220 KV bays to be utilized
for evacuation of power share from the Thein dam. The Punjab Government
had been insisting that cost of bays be borne by the State Government since
the year 1996 onwards. The stalemate continued and the dispute could not be
settled in-spite of interventions by the CEA and Northern Zonal Council
during 2003-04. Due to failure of the State Government to provide हैं 4.50
crore on account of cost of two 220 KV bays, the State could not draw its
power share from the Thein dam.

Thus, inaction of the department to take decision for evacuation of power
from the Thein dam hydro electric power project for the last three decades
resulted in non utilization of 220 KV double circuit Thein-Hiranagar
transmission line and consequent idle investment of हैं 25.73 crore. The

immediate restoration of transmission system in the event of major failures.

manpower. The DG sets and synchroscopes'” form part of Disaster
management facilities at EHT sub-stations connecting major generating
stations. Audit noticed that no disaster management setup existed in the State
for immediate restoration of transmission system in the event of any major
failure.

A test-check (April 2012) of records further revealed that out of 54 Grid sub-
stations DG sets were available only in 37 (68 per cent) sub-stations. Further,
snychroscopes were provided in five’! Sub-stations out of which one’? was
non-functional.

The Chief Engineers, S&O wings, Kashmir as well as Jammu admitted
(April/July 2012) that the Disaster management cell had not been setup due
to paucity of funds and that no emergency restoration systems were available

2.3.17.2 Avoidable expenditure

As per the Centrally Electricity Regulatory Commission (terms and
conditions of tariff) Regulation Notification of March 2001 as amended from
January 2008, a rebate of two per cent is allowable for payment of bills of
capacity charges and energy charges through letter of credit (LC). However,
in case the payments are made by a mode other than through the letter of
credit but within a period of one month of presentation of bills by the
generating company, a rebate of one per cent is allowable. Further, in case
the bills are delayed by the beneficiaries beyond a period of one month from
the date of billing, a late payment surcharge at the rate of 1.5 per cent per
month shall be levied by the generating company.

Audit scrutiny (June 2012) of records revealed that despite the fact that State,
being dependent on procurement of power from outside sources, the
Department had not taken benefit of this facility. The system of payment of
power bills by operation of LC though started during the year 2008-09 had
not been adopted by the Department. However as per the procedure in vogue
the bills raised by the power supplier are received by the Executive Engineer,
Load Dispatch and Meter Testing (LD&MT) Division, Jammu and after
verification are forwarded to the Executive Engineer, Commercial Survey
Division, Jammu for onward transmission to the Administrative Department
(Civil Secretariat) and to the State Finance Department for financial
provisions. After passing through all these stages, the bills are then returned
back to the Executive Engineer, LD&MT Division, Jammu for to payment.
The Department had not thus availed the rebate of two per cent for release of
payments though LC. Even the benefit of payment of power bills within one
month for availing one per cent rebate was also not taken by the Department
to the full extent. Audit further noticed that during the period 2007-08 to
2011-12 the Department had availed of rebate of हैं 22.55 crore only against
the allowable rebate of € 190.64 crore resulting in avoidable payment of
र₹ 168.07 crore. Further, due to delayed payment of power bills = 45.90 crore
had been paid by the Department as late payment surcharge during the period
from 2007-08 to 2011-12 resulting in further extra avoidable expenditure to
that extent.

The Executive Engineer, SLDC stated (June 2012) that prior to March 2011
sanctions for opening of LCs for payment to various CPSUs/Power
supplying agencies were accorded and from April 2011 the funds were
placed at the disposal of the Division which was later dispensed with by the
Government. However, the reasons for dispensing with the practice of
payment through LC were not furnished to audit.

2.3.19 Manpower Management

The power utility was required to devise different modules of training for
their staff to update their knowledge based on the latest development in the
respective fields. The Department was also required to have a well defined
HRD policy and systems. Based on requisitions, inputs from various
transmission utility divisions, the staff particularly the technicians and Junior
Engineers entrusted with manning of substations and EHV transmission lines
were required to be got equipped with adequate skills to ensure smooth and
safe operation and maintenance of transmission system of the Department.

Audit observed (April/July 2012) that a strength of 485 technicians was
required in four utility divisions of Jammu region for operationalising and
maintaining 18 Grid sub-stations, against which only 350 technicians were in
position and there was a shortage of 135 (28 per cent) technicians for
manning these Grid sub-stations. Similarly, there was an overall shortage of
technical staff to the extent of 18 per cent in Kashmir region. Audit further
noticed that no trainings were found imparted to the technical staff during the
period 2007-08 to 2011-12. Thus, the manpower management was below par
due to shortage of technicians required for manning transmission
infrastructure and also because of not imparting training to the technicians.

The Chief Engineers, S&O Wing, Kashmir as well as Jammu admitted
(July/September 2012) that no system of trainings and up gradation of skills
existed in the Department because of non availability of funds and
acknowledged the need for adopting the system on the lines of Power Grid
Corporation India Limited (PGCIL) and National Hydro-Electric Power
Corporation (NHPC).

2.3.21 Conclusion

The State had not been able to take full advantage of the assistance given by
the Government of India as it had not been able to implement the projects in
a time bound manner. Plan funds to the extent of 49 per cent only were
utilized by the Department during the period 2007-08 to 2011-12. A State
Electricity Plan and State Electricity Policy, as provided in the Jammu and
Kashmir Electricity Act, 2010, to give shape to the future requirements in the
Transmission Sector and to provide a roadmap for development of Power
system in the State, had not been formulated despite lapse of about two years.
The Department had failed to achieve the planned targets during 2007-12 and
almost all the Grid sub-station and Transmission line projects started under
Prime Minister’s Reconstruction Plan (PMRP) had witnessed a time overrun.
Some of the completed projects could not be operationalised due to
incompletion of other related works with the result the infrastructure created
was lying idle. The projects had suffered due to unplanned project
formulations, execution of projects on adhoc basis and execution of projects
without availability of essential pre-planning stage components like land,
Right of Way, well formulated structural designs, site conditions, sound bid
evaluation, etc. The transmission losses exceeded the Central Electricity
Authority (CEA) norm of four per cent and ranged between 5.07 and 8.14
per cent during the period 2008-09 to 2011-12. In-efficient Grid
management had led to payment of Unscheduled Interchage (UD) charges to
the Northern Regional Electricity Board (NREB). The Department failed to
install Power Factor (PF) correction capacitor banks resulted in payment of &
220.65 crore on account of ‘Reactive Energy’ charges during the period
2002-03 to 2011-12. Against requirement of = 160.65 crore for maintenance
of transmission assets, € 36.33 crore was provided during the period 2007-08
to 2011-12 indicating ignorance of the Department in the maintenance of the
assets. The Department did not setup Disaster Management system in all the
power utilities in the State due to paucity of funds.

241 Introduction

Government of India (GOI) enacted (August 1996)' the Building and Other
Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act,
1996 (BOCW Act) for constitution of a Welfare Board in each State to undertake
social security schemes”. The GOI also enacted (August 1996)? the Building and
Other Construction Workers Welfare Cess Act, 1996 (Cess Act). Section 14 of the
Cess Act stipulates that rule making power under the Act vests only with the GOI.
The GOI framed (March 1998) the Building and other Construction Workers Welfare
Cess Rules, 1998 (Cess Rules). To augment the resources of the Board, Section 3 of
the Cess Act as amended in September 1996 provided for levy and collection of
labour welfare cess at a uniform rate of one percent of the cost of construction
incurred by the employer. For the safety, health and welfare of the workers, the State
Government in pursuance of sections 40 and 62 of the BOCW Act also framed
(uly 2006) the Jammu and Kashmir Building and Other Construction Workers
(Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 2006 (J&KBOCW
Rules) as amended in November 2012. The State Government constituted (July 2007)
the Jammu and Kashmir Building and Other Construction Workers Welfare Board
(Board) to carry out welfare schemes for construction workers. The provisions of
BOCW Act are applicable to every establishment which employs, or had employed on
any day of the preceding 12 months, 10 or more workers in any building or other
construction works. All such establishments engaged in construction activity are
liable to pay cess under the Cess Act except construction activity by an employer in
relation to his residence costing less than हैं 10 lakh (excluding the cost of land).

2.4.2 Organisational set-up

To oversee the implementation of the BOCW and Cess Acts, the State Government
had appointed (January 2007) the Labour Commissioner of the State as Chief
Inspector and Appellate Authority, two Deputy Labour Commissioners as Assessing
Officers (one each for Kashmir and Jammu province), 22 Assistant Labour
Commissioners as Registering Officers/ Cess Collectors and 24 Labour Officers as
Inspectors for the whole State within their respective jurisdiction.

The Board is headed by the Hon’ble Minister of Labour and Employment as
Chairman. The other members of the Board are Welfare Commissioner (Hgr.),
Ministry of Labour and Employment, GOI and 15 representatives, five each from the
State Government, employers and workers. The Secretary of the Board was an officer
of State Government of the rank of Deputy Secretary (October 2012).

2.4.7.3 Registration of establishments

Section 7 of the BOCW Act 1996 provides that every employer is required to make an
application with prescribed fee for the registration of his establishment within a period
of sixty days of the commencement of the Act or within sixty days from the date on
which Act becomes applicable to the establishment. The Board is also required under
Section 43(a) of the Act ibid to identify all the Government agencies and private
builders falling within the purview of the Act and arrange to collect cess at prescribed
rates. The cess is to be collected from every employer in such manner and at such
time including deduction at source in relation to a building or other construction work
of a Government or of a public sector undertaking or advance collection through a
local authority where an approval of such building or other construction work by such
local authority is required. Besides, the Board is required under Cess Act to educate
the employers about penalties, fine and imprisonment for violation and contravention
of the Acts. But it was noticed that neither list of registered employers was available
with the Board nor the Board had conducted any such exercise to identify the
employers as no such consolidated information was available in the Board office.

The State Labour Commissioner (Chief Inspector of Inspection under the Act) had,
however, identified 88 defaulting employers and list thereof was furnished (October
2011) to Commissioner/ Secretary, Labour and Employment Department. Though
notices had been served by the cess collectors of Kashmir division in 40 cases, no
action had been taken in Jammu division in respect of 48 defaulting cases. The
Secretary stated (August 2012) that assessing officers and cess collectors had been
requested to gear up the process of recovery of cess from the defaulters. It was also
stated that an amount of € 4.85 crore was received from an employer but position of
recovery of cess from the 88 cases pointed out in audit was not intimated.

2.4.10 Monitoring mechanism

The Board had empowered (July 2011) the CEO/ Secretary to take up the process of
implementation of the scheme by constituting committees at district level for
monitoring the implementation of the Act in an effective manner, Such committees
were to meet at regular intervals to give necessary feedback to the Board for removal
of the difficulties in smooth implementation of the scheme. Out of 22 monitoring
committees, only four committees (Reasi, Samba, Ganderbal and Kargil) had
furnished feedback to the Board. Thus, the very purpose of constitution of district
level committees for the better implementation of the Act could not be achieved. The
Secretary stated (August 2012) that the matter had been taken up with all the District
Commissioners and only some of them had shown keen interest in implementing the
Act. Audit further noticed that no meetings were conducted by the ALCs with the
district heads, etc. with regard to the implementation of the Act as no such reports
were on record with the ALCs.

2411 Conclusion

The State Government started implementation of the BOCW and Cess Acts after a
delay of more than 11 years from their enactments. The J&K Building and Other
Construction Workers Welfare Board after its constitution in March 2007 did not take
any initiatives to formulate the modalities for implementing the welfare schemes till
February 2011. The State Advisory Committee was not constituted even after more
than 16 years of enactment of the Act to advice the Board on such matters arising out
of the administration of the Act, as may be referred to it. The crucial aspects of
identification of beneficiaries and registration of establishments and implementation
of welfare schemes for workers were not given due priority. As a result, huge funds to
the extent of हैं 100.62 crore remained unutilised with the Board as of March 2012.
Expenditure to the tune of = 73.22 lakh had been incurred in excess of the permissible
limit during 2010-12 on establishment and other expenditure in contravention of the
Act. The monitoring mechanism was weak and internal audit and internal control
system had also not been instituted by the Board.

2.5. Fraudulent drawals

Non-observance of prescribed checks by the Principal, Government Girls
Higher Secondary School and Treasury Officer, Bhaderwah facilitated
fraudulent drawals of % 3.26 lakh.

Rule 2.27 of the Jammu and Kashmir Financial Code provide that the disbursing
officer should enter all bills drawn from the Treasury for departmental expenditure in
a register and get all drawals verified with the registers maintained at the Treasury
once in a month. Further, the rules stipulate that all monetary transactions should be
entered in the cash book as soon as they occur and should be attested by the Head of
the office in token of check.

The procedure for drawal of money from Treasury involves the following steps:

a. preparation and submission of the bills duly attested by the Drawing and
Disbursing Officer (DDO) to the Treasury;

b transferring of money by the Treasury into the official account of the DDO
and recording the entry of payment by the Treasury Officer in treasury records viz.,
Register in Form-3 (Madhwar);

०. recording of the entries of drawal of money by the DDO in his drawal register
and cash book and

व्‌. periodical reconciliation of the cash book balances with the drawal register
and the Bank account statement by the DDO. For this purpose, the DDO is to obtain
from the Treasury Officer by the 15" of every month, a list of bills drawn during the
previous month and trace them in the cash book.

Audit check (December 2010) of records of the Principal, Government Girls Higher
Secondary School, Bhaderwah (DDO) by way of verification of transactions recorded
in the drawal register with the Bank Account statement of the DDO and the records of
Treasury Bhaderwah revealed that three drawals' amounting to हैं 2.46 lakh were
drawn (January 2009 and February 2010) from the Treasury and had not been
recorded in drawal register and cash book of the DDO. These drawals were made on
the basis of fictitious claims of General Provident Fund (GPF) advance (% 1.30 lakh)
of two officials and pay arrears of the staff (¥ 1.16 lakh) from the Treasury. The
entries thereof were not recorded in the drawal register, cash book and GPF advance
register of the office or the personal records of the employees. The amounts after
transfer by the treasury to the official account of the DDO were subsequently credited
to the bank accounts of a fake official (January 2009) and senior assistant of the office
(February 2010) respectively on the basis of authority letters issued by the DDO. A
check of treasury records (Madhwar) and the drawal register revealed that the
Treasury Officer without verifying the drawals made by the DDO during January
2009 and February 2010 from his records had recorded wrong certificates of
verification of drawals on the drawal register.

' January 2009: ₹ 0.70 lakh; January 2009: ₹ 0.60 lakh and February 2010: ₹ 1.16 lakh

The matter was pointed out (December 2010) in Audit to the Principal, Government

Thus, non-observance of prescribed checks by the Principal, Government Girls
Higher Secondary School and Treasury Officer, Bhaderwah facilitated fraudulent
drawals of = 3.26 lakh by the DDO. The risk of drawal of GPF advances on fake bills
may be minimised by establishing a system of intimating to the concerned employee

2.21 INDUSTRIES AND COMMERCE DEPARTMENT

The Industries and Commerce Department is responsible for promotion of
growth of industries, creation of new employment opportunities and
development of new designs in the Handloom and Handicraft sectors in the
State, besides optimum and sustainable usage of State mineral resources. A
Chief Controlling Officer-based audit of the Department brought to fore several
areas of concern: (a) Departmental failure of non-existent oversight resulting in
low industrial output, low employment generation, low-end and low value-
addition manufacturing despite fiscal burden of about € 8340 crore on the State
and Central exchequer during 2007-12, thus, defeating the objectives of the
Central/State Governments’ industrial promotion policies, (b) under-utilisation
of Central assistance, (c) unplanned execution of industrial estates/growth
centres, leading to unproductive investments, (d) inadmissible and irregular
payment of subsidies, VAT reimbursement and irregular exemption of toll tax,
(e) under-utilisation of training centres. Audit also noticed that performance of
implementation of schemes in Handicrafts and Handloom sector was poor and
the purpose of imparting training to unemployed persons for generating
employment through formation of co-operative societies was not achieved. The
Department had no mechanism in place to check the quantities of minerals
extracted and lifted by the lessees from the mineral sites.

2.21.7 Planning

Proper planning is essential for success of the programme. The District Industries
Centres (DICs) were required to conduct and update the industrial survey of the
districts for assessing the industrial potential including availability of human
resources and raw material, marketing avenues and other factors for preparation of
Perspective Plan and Annual Plans at periodical intervals. Audit scrutiny revealed
that no such survey was conducted by the DICs of the Department. The Director,
Industries and Commerce, Jammu stated (July 2012) that the General Managers of
respective DICs would be asked to conduct such surveys. The Joint Director
Development, Directorate of Industries and Commerce, Kashmir, however, stated
(August 2012) that such surveys were conducted while identifying land for industrial
estates through field agencies. The Commissioner/Secretary reported (December
2012) that fresh potential survey had been conducted and communicated to the
Government of India by the District Industries Centres of the Kashmir valley. The
reply should be viewed in light of the fact that General Managers of three test-
checked DICs (Srinagar, Baramulla and Anantnag) had stated that no such survey
was conducted in the districts.

To accelerate industrial development of the State and boost investor-confidence, the
Government of India sanctioned special package of incentives in June 2002. To
supplement this, the State Government had also sanctioned (January 2004) its own
package of incentives under the State Industrial Policy 2004. One of the objectives
of State Industrial Policy 2004 was to generate 90 per cent employment in the
industrial units. The Department was not monitoring whether the industrial units set
up under the Central/State Government’ s industrial promotion policies and provided
with fiscal incentives and subsidies were indeed meeting the objective of
employment generation as laid down in the State Industrial Policy 2004. The
employment generated data was accepted as claimed by the industrial units without
any mechanism for verification being in place. There is no mechanism in place to
monitor the turnover, value of output, profitability, extent and quality of
employment generation, actual new investment brought in and extent of value
addition in the manufacturing by the units so as to see whether these are
commensurate with the burden of tax concessions and subsidies on the public
exchequer besides, facilitating balanced geographically well-dispersed growth as
evident from the succeeding paragraphs

2.21.21.1 Integrated Handloom Development Scheme

To facilitate the sustainable development of handloom weavers located in or outside

% 5.91 crore) and 17 Group Approach Projects (estimated cost: % 1.21 crore) were
sanctioned by the GOI during 2007-08 and 2009-11 respectively. For the cluster
projects of the scheme, the guidelines envisage formation of consortium involving
stake holders from the Self Help Groups (SHGs), co-operative societies, master
weavers, private entrepreneurs, NGOs for interaction with the weavers, etc.

To ensure regular availability of yarn of requisite count and to avoid delay in
production process, one time assistance of & three lakh per cluster was to be provided
as a corpus fund to National Handloom Development Corporation (NHDC) to ensure
supply of yarn to the weavers against payment through yarn depots at the cluster.
Further, to provide facilities of pre-loom and post-loom operations, quality control
laboratory, common work shed, water treatment and effluent treatment plants to
weavers, common facility centre was to be set up in each cluster.

It was noticed that consortium was formed from weavers of the area only and did not
involve SHGs, private entrepreneurs, cooperative societies and NGOs. The Assistant
Director, Handlooms Kathua stated (July 2012) that necessary steps would be taken to
include SHGs, NGOs, private entrepreneurs, etc. in the consortium.

Further, no yarn depot was set up and no corpus fund was maintained in any of the

was also utilized for imparting training and for making samples which defeated the

2.21.28 Illegal mining

The Environment Protection Act, 1986 provides that no mining should be carried out
in wildlife reserve area. The Hon’ble Supreme Court of India notified (December
2006) areas falling within 10 kilometers of the boundary of National Park and
Wildlife Sanctuaries as eco-sensitive zones and extraction of minerals in such areas
was prohibited. The Department however, did not adhere to the provisions of the Act
and the directions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court and instead granted mining lease to
lessees for extraction of Gypsum within and in the vicinity of Kazinag National Park
and Limber-Lachipora Wildlife Sanctuary despite reservations raised (April/October
2010) by the Ministry of Environment and Forests (Wildlife Division), Government
of India and Commissioner/Secretary to the State Government, Forest Department. It

2.21.33 Monitoring and Evaluation

2.21.35 Conclusion

The employment generation and value addition by the industrial units getting fiscal
concessions and subsidies from Central and State Governments was not
commensurate with the burden of exchequer. These beneficiary units were also not
geographically well-dispersed, concentrated around railheads closer to neighbouring
States. There were cases of diversion/misutilisation of funds towards payment of
salaries/wages, etc. Overpayments/irregular payments to entrepreneurs were noticed
due to non-observance of guidelines/instructions governing packages of incentives.
The performance of various Central Schemes in Handicraft and Handloom sector was
poor. There was lack of adequate monitoring of training centres. The Department had
no mechanism in place to check the quantities of minerals extracted and lifted by the
lessees from the mineral sites.

Chapter-3 : Revenue Sector : General
3.1 Introduction

Under Sectoral re-organisation, there are five departments, Finance, Law, Power,
Transport and Revenue of the Government which have been included under the
Revenue Sector. These relate to Tax revenue. The other 24 departments falling under
Social Sector, General Sector and Economic Sector contributes Non-Tax revenue.
The major areas of Tax receipts are Tax on sale/ trade, Taxes on services administered
by the Commissioner Commercial Taxes, State Excise administered by the Excise
Commissioner, Stamp Duty and Registration Fees, Taxes and Duties on Electricity,
Taxes on Vehicles etc. and the major areas of Non-Tax revenue are from Power,
Interest receipts, Dividends, Forestry and Wild Life, Public Works, Water supply and
Sanitation. Out of these departments, audit was conducted in 61 units of three
departments out of 173 local auditable units by the Revenue Sector and during the
year 2011-12, audit had pointed out underassessment/short levy/loss of revenue
aggregating to ~ 42.09 crore in 255 cases. The concerned departments accepted
underassessment and other deficiencies of € 5.24 crore involved in 50 cases.

3.1.1 Audit mandate

The audit of revenue receipts of the State Government is conducted under Section 16
of the Comptroller and Auditor's General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of
Service) Act, 1971.

3.1.2 Audit planning

The unit offices under various Departments are categorized into high, medium and
low risk units according to their revenue position, past trends of audit observations
and other parameters. The annual audit plan is prepared on the basis of risk analysis
which inter alia includes critical issues in Government revenues and tax
administration i.e. budget speech, Reports of the Finance Commission (State and
Central), recommendations of the Taxation Reforms Committee, statistical analysis of
the revenue earnings during the past five years, factors of the tax administration, audit
coverage and its impact during past five years, etc.

During the year 2011-12, 61 units out of 173 auditable units were planned and
audited, which is 35 per cent of the total auditable units.

3.9 Response of the Departments/Government towards audit

Principal Accountant General (Audit) Jammu and Kashmir (PAG), conducts
periodical inspection of the Government Departments to test check the transactions
and verify the maintenance of the important accounts and other records as prescribed
in the rules. These inspections are followed up with Inspection Reports (IRs)
incorporating irregularities detected during the inspection and not settled on the spot,
which were issued to the heads of the offices with copies to the next higher authorities
for taking prompt corrective action. The Heads of offices/Government are required to
comply promptly with the observations contained in the IRs, rectify the defects and
omissions and report compliance through initial reply to the PAG’s office within one
month from the date of receipt of the IRs. Serious financial irregularities are reported to
the heads of the Departments and the Government.

representatives of the people in the form of quality mid-term/end-term appraisals of
various socio-economic programmes funded by the exchequer or of reliable assurance
on compliance with relevant rules and principles prescribed for incurring or collecting

4.1.8 Revenue potential of the Tax on Services under the State Law vis-a-vis
foregone share of the State in the Central Service Tax

Service Tax is the only Central tax that is presently not applicable to the State of
Jammu & Kashmir because, unlike other States, Jammu and Kashmir levies tax on
services under its own law, viz., the Jammu and Kashmir General Sales Tax (GST)
Act, 1962. Hence, the State gets a share in all Central taxes/duties except in the total

regarding likely (Central) Service Tax collection during 2010-15, the 1.551 per cent
share foregone by the State of Jammu and Kashmir works out to % 8363.38 crore.
During 2010-11, the State’s foregone share in Central Service Tax was about हैं 1100
crore whereas the total collection by the State on ‘Services’ under the J&K GST Act

revenue gain to the State exchequer from the tax on pure services collected from non-

than the share in the Central Service Tax being foregone by the State.
